What is the Grand Strategy Matrix?

The Grand Strategy Matrix is a strategic management tool used to help organizations identify suitable strategies based on their current position in the market.

It answers two important questions:

  • Is the market growing fast or slow?
  • Is the company competitively strong or weak?

Based on these two answers, the organization is placed into one of four quadrants. Each quadrant suggests a different strategic direction.

💡 In simple words: The Grand Strategy Matrix helps a company decide whether it should expand, improve, survive, or diversify.

Teaching Note

Look at the matrix first. Do not memorize the quadrant name. Just ask: Is the market high or low growth, and is the company strong or weak?

5 Questions
Two Main Dimensions

Market Growth

Market growth refers to whether the industry or market is expanding, stable, saturated, or declining.

High-Growth Market

  • Increasing customer demand
  • New opportunities
  • Rising industry interest
  • Room for expansion
  • Growing customer segments

Low-Growth Market

  • Slow demand
  • Saturated competition
  • Limited new customers
  • Declining interest
  • Reduced expansion opportunities
⚠️ Avoid saying: "Book market is dead."
Better: "The traditional physical bookstore market faces slower growth, but selected niche segments may still have demand."

Competitive Position

Competitive position refers to how strong the organization is compared to its competitors.

Strong Position

  • Strong brand recognition
  • Loyal customers
  • Clear market positioning
  • Good location
  • Strong product range
  • Strong online presence

Weak Position

  • Low brand awareness
  • Weak digital presence
  • Limited product variety
  • Poor customer experience
  • Weak marketing
  • Outdated business model

Bookstore Examples

BrandCompetitive Position
POPULAR MalaysiaStrong — broad product range, school materials, stationery, mass-market familiarity
MPH BookstoresRecognizable brand, but may need stronger strategic repositioning
Kinokuniya MalaysiaStrong niche and premium bookstore experience
Pustaka MukminNiche strength in religious/academic books, but faces scale and digital pressure

The Four Quadrants

The Grand Strategy Matrix has four quadrants based on two dimensions: market growth and competitive position.

Quadrant I · Strong + High Growth
EXPAND
Best position. Push forward with growth strategies.
Quadrant II · Weak + High Growth
IMPROVE
Market is attractive. Fix competitiveness first.
Quadrant III · Weak + Low Growth
SURVIVE / RETRENCH
Weakest position. Reduce risk and restructure.
Quadrant IV · Strong + Low Growth
DIVERSIFY
Still strong. Find new direction for future growth.
🧠 Quick memory: QI = Expand · QII = Improve · QIII = Survive · QIV = Diversify
Quadrant I: Expand

Strong Position + High Market Growth

Quadrant I is the most favorable position. The company is strong, and the market is also growing. The company has a strong chance to grow further because it has internal capability and external opportunity.

Suitable Strategies

  • Market penetration
  • Market development
  • Product development
  • Expansion
  • Stronger online platform
  • Strategic partnership

Example: POPULAR Malaysia

POPULAR may be placed in Quadrant I if the focus is on education-related retail, school books, assessment books, stationery, and student learning materials.

  • Strong brand familiarity
  • Wide product range
  • Serves students, parents, teachers, and general readers
  • Demand for education support materials still exists
  • Can grow through online sales, school partnerships, and membership campaigns
Sample Answer: POPULAR Malaysia can be placed in Quadrant I if the education and stationery market is considered growing and the company has a strong competitive position. Suitable strategies include market penetration, product development, online expansion, and stronger school-based partnerships.
📌 Teaching Line: Quadrant I means the company is strong, and the market still has room to grow. So, push forward.

5 Questions
Quadrant II: Improve

Weak Position + High Market Growth

Quadrant II means the market is attractive, but the company is not strong enough to fully benefit from it. The opportunity exists, but the organization must improve its competitiveness.

Suitable Strategies

  • Improve competitiveness
  • Strengthen branding
  • Improve online presence
  • Improve customer experience
  • Product improvement
  • Repositioning
  • Strategic partnership

Example: Pustaka Mukmin / Kedai Buku Pustaka

May be placed in Quadrant II if the niche market is still growing, but the company has weaker competitive reach.

  • Demand may still exist for Islamic books, school books, academic books, or exam materials
  • May have niche knowledge and loyal customers
  • But may lack strong digital marketing
  • May have limited online sales reach
  • May struggle against larger chains and online marketplaces
Sample Answer: Pustaka Mukmin may be placed in Quadrant II if its niche book segment still has demand, but its competitive position is weaker. Suitable strategies include improving online presence, strengthening niche branding, and developing targeted customer communities.
📌 Teaching Line: Quadrant II means the opportunity is there, but the company must fix its position first.

5 Questions
Quadrant III: Survive

Weak Position + Low Market Growth

Quadrant III is the weakest position. The company is weak, and the market is also slow or declining. The organization must be careful because growth opportunities are limited and survival becomes the priority.

Suitable Strategies

  • Cost reduction
  • Restructuring
  • Retrenchment
  • Downsizing
  • Divestiture
  • Exit strategy
  • Business transformation

Example: Small Outdated Bookstore

A small outdated bookstore may be placed in Quadrant III if:

  • Walk-in customers are declining
  • The store has weak branding
  • It has no online platform
  • Product selection is outdated
  • Younger customers prefer online purchasing
⚠️ This does not always mean immediate closure. It means the business must reduce risk and rethink its model.
Sample Answer: A small outdated bookstore may be placed in Quadrant III because it has a weak competitive position in a slow physical bookstore market. Suitable strategies include cost reduction, restructuring, online transformation, or focusing on a smaller profitable niche.
📌 Teaching Line: Quadrant III means stop the bleeding first before thinking about growth.

Check Your Understanding

5 Questions
Quadrant IV: Diversify

Strong Position + Low Market Growth

Quadrant IV means the company is strong, but the market is slow, mature, or saturated. The company still has resources and brand strength, but the current market may not provide enough future growth.

Suitable Strategies

  • Diversification
  • New product categories
  • New customer segments
  • New markets
  • Digital transformation
  • Related business expansion
  • Events and services

Example 1: Kinokuniya Malaysia

Kinokuniya may be placed in Quadrant IV if we consider the physical bookstore market as slower, while Kinokuniya still has strong niche positioning.

  • Strong premium bookstore identity
  • Strong customer experience
  • Curated international book selection
  • But physical book retail may face slower growth
Sample Answer: Kinokuniya Malaysia may be placed in Quadrant IV because it has strong niche positioning and brand identity, but the physical bookstore market is slower due to online purchasing and digital reading. Diversification into events, curated experiences, and online community engagement is suitable.

Example 2: MPH Bookstores

MPH may also be placed in Quadrant IV if it still has brand recognition but operates in a slower physical bookstore market. Suitable strategies:

  • Strengthen online bookstore
  • School and corporate supply
  • Book events
  • Stationery and lifestyle expansion
  • Smaller experience-based store formats
📌 Teaching Line: Quadrant IV means the company is still strong, but the market is getting tired. So, find new direction.

Matrix Comparisons

Grand Strategy Matrix vs BCG Matrix

Students may confuse these two because both use four quadrants. But the focus is different.

AspectGrand Strategy MatrixBCG Matrix
Main purposeSelect overall strategy directionAnalyze product or business portfolio
Main focusCompany or business positionProduct / SBU performance
Dimension 1Market GrowthMarket Growth Rate
Dimension 2Competitive PositionRelative Market Share
OutputExpand, Improve, Survive, DiversifyStar, Cash Cow, Question Mark, Dog
🔑 Grand Strategy Matrix = Where should the company go?
🔑 BCG Matrix = Which product/business unit deserves attention?

Grand Strategy Matrix vs SPACE Matrix

AspectSPACE MatrixGrand Strategy Matrix
DimensionsFS, IS, CA, ESMarket growth + competitive position
CalculationHas scoring and calculationUsually no calculation
OutputAggressive, Competitive, Conservative, DefensiveExpand, Improve, Survive, Diversify
NatureMore technicalMore conceptual
🔑 SPACE Matrix = Can we push, fight, maintain, or defend?
🔑 Grand Strategy Matrix = Should we expand, improve, survive, or diversify?

Common Mistakes

Avoid these common errors in your analysis and answers.

Mistake 1: Confusing market growth with company popularity

Wrong "Kinokuniya is famous, so market growth is high."
Better Kinokuniya may have strong competitive position, but market growth must be judged based on the bookstore industry or selected book retail segment.

Mistake 2: Thinking strong company always means Quadrant I

Remember A company can be strong but operate in a slow market. That is Quadrant IV, not Quadrant I.

Mistake 3: Thinking Quadrant III means immediate closure

Remember Quadrant III means the organization must survive, restructure, reduce cost, or transform. Closure is only one possible option.

Mistake 4: Giving strategy without justification

Weak "MPH should diversify because it is famous."
Better "MPH should diversify because it has brand recognition, but the traditional physical bookstore market faces slower growth due to online purchasing and changing reading habits."

Answer Template

Use this structure when answering Grand Strategy Matrix questions in assignments or exams.

The company can be placed in Quadrant ___ because it has ___ market growth and a ___ competitive position.

This is shown by ___ and ___.

Therefore, the suitable strategy is ___ because ___.

Worked Example: Kinokuniya

Kinokuniya Malaysia can be placed in Quadrant IV because it has a strong competitive position but operates in a slower physical bookstore market.

This is shown by its premium bookstore identity and curated book selection, while the market faces pressure from online book purchasing and digital reading.

Therefore, suitable strategies include diversification into events, exclusive collections, online communities, and premium customer experiences.

🎯 Key lesson: Strategy is not about guessing the quadrant. Strategy is about justifying why the company belongs there and what action fits best.
Class Activity

📚 Bookstore Strategy Battle

Divide students into four groups. Each group is assigned a bookstore brand.

Group 1
POPULAR Malaysia
Group 2
MPH Bookstores
Group 3
Kinokuniya Malaysia
Group 4
Pustaka Mukmin / Kedai Buku Pustaka

Each Group Must Answer:

  • Is the market growth high or low?
  • Is the competitive position strong or weak?
  • Which quadrant fits?
  • What strategy should the company choose?
  • Defend the answer with evidence.

Pressure Questions 🔥

Why do you say the market is high growth?
Is the brand strong, or just familiar?
What hidden risk does the bookstore face?
Is diversification suitable, or should the company improve first?
What happens if online competitors become stronger?
✅ Remember: Different assumptions may lead to different strategic conclusions — and that is acceptable, as long as the reasoning is justified.
